title: 3-Read Friday #5: Teach Like No One Is Listening, Marginal Gains, and Exterior Angles
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue five brings together three posts on checking, refining, and deepening classroom practice. Barton leads with Craig Latimir's "Dance Like Nobody's Watching," praising the mindset of assuming no student has listened or understood until there's evidence otherwise, which he calls "a super-powerful mindset." He then covers Thahmina Begum's "100 things 1% better," which takes the marginal-gains idea popularized by British Cycling and applies it concretely to something as small as dismissing a class, a move Barton contrasts with the "abstract and gimmicky" way marginal gains is usually pitched in CPD. He closes with the first installment of Paul Rowlandson's three-part series on interior and exterior angles, calling Rowlandson "one of my all-time favourite maths bloggers" for his topic-specific deep dives. All three items are fundamentally about pedagogy and instructional technique, anchoring this issue in Learning & Curriculum.
points: Barton elevates Latimir's "teach like nobody is listening" mantra as a mindset shift rather than a technique, distinguishing it from simply lowering expectations.
He contrasts Begum's concrete, 13-component breakdown of a single classroom routine with the usual "abstract and gimmicky" CPD treatment of marginal gains.
He flags that Rowlandson's post taught him something about exterior angles he "hadn't thought about in 30 years," underscoring the piece's value even for an experienced maths teacher.
quotes: In this post, Craig explains why he teaches like nobody is listening.
Unless he has evidence that students have both listened and understood, he assumes they haven’t. This is a super-powerful mindset to have as a teacher.
Teaching can’t resist a bandwagon, and hence I remember sitting through several CPD sessions where we were advised to seek out the marginal gains in our lessons and exploit them.
In this post, Thahmina goes concrete and super-specific, identifying 13 components of how she dismisses a class at the end of the lesson and seeks out ways to make a 1% improvement in each of them.
Paul tackles the topic of interior and exterior angles, suggesting we use something that I haven’t thought about in 30 years
